properties.headline: Flooding under marsh vegetation is spreading at Lake Manzala
properties.subtitle: Coastal lagoon and reed beds
properties.confidence_note: Exploratory dB thresholds on L-band backscatter, not a validated flood map
properties.summary: Radar measured 2.6% of the analysed area as flooded vegetation on 12 October 2026. That is more than the 2.4% measured on 26 June 2026. Flooded vegetation looks very bright to radar: water and plant stems form a corner that bounces the signal straight back, while the cross-polarised signal stays weak.
causes: Water rising into standing reeds and marsh vegetation
Seasonal flooding of fish farms and marsh margins
Vegetation growing up through shallow standing water
properties.why_it_matters: Lake Manzala is one of Egypt's largest coastal wetlands. How much of it is open water and how much is flooded marsh decides what fishing, farming and wildlife it can support.
properties.next_step: Compare with optical imagery and local water-level records before treating the change as confirmed.
properties.explanation:
NISAR passed over Lake Manzala 9 times between 26 June 2026 and 12 October 2026, all from the same track and look direction so the measurements can be compared. Each pass records two polarisations, HH and HV. Flooded vegetation looks very bright to radar: water and plant stems form a corner that bounces the signal straight back, while the cross-polarised signal stays weak. Pixels brighter than -5 dB in HH whose HH is more than 7 dB above their HV are counted as flooded vegetation.

Across those passes the share of the analysed area classed as flooded vegetation grew from 2.4% to 2.6%, a change of +0.2 percentage points. The lowest reading was 2.3% on 8 July 2026 and the highest 3.4% on 18 September 2026, a trend of about +0.2 percentage points per month. The outline on the map is every part of the area that was flooded vegetation in at least one month, and it covers about 11 km².

What this does not say: these are threshold rules on radar brightness, not a verified flood map. Wind roughening the water surface, wet soil after rain and a different look angle can all move the same numbers. Short, sharp changes between two passes are more likely to be weather or geometry than real change on the ground.

Why it matters: Lake Manzala is one of Egypt's largest coastal wetlands. How much of it is open water and how much is flooded marsh decides what fishing, farming and wildlife it can support. Compare with optical imagery and local water-level records before treating the change as confirmed.

properties.headline: Ground sinking along the northern Delta coast
properties.subtitle: Coastal farmland
properties.summary: The radar shows this land sinking a little more with every pass. The drop is steady, not sudden, so it isn't from a single event.
causes: Soft delta soil slowly settling
Groundwater pumped for farms and towns
properties.why_it_matters: Low fields near the coast become more exposed to seawater and flooding.
properties.next_step: Compare with groundwater and land-use records for this area.
properties.explanation:
Between January and October the radar measured the ground along this stretch of coast dropping by about 6.7 millimetres, which is a rate of roughly 8 millimetres per year.

The sinking is smooth and continuous. A sudden event such as an earthquake would show up as a sharp step, and there is none here. That pattern is consistent with slow settling of soft delta soil, possibly made faster by groundwater being pumped out.

Why it matters: the Delta is already very flat. Even small drops can let seawater reach farmland more easily. This is an early signal to check against groundwater and land-use records, not a confirmed cause.

properties.headline: Soil moisture shifting across mid-Delta farmland
properties.subtitle: Irrigated cropland
properties.confidence_note: Seasonal irrigation may explain part of this
properties.summary: Radar signals from these fields rise and fall in rhythm with the season. Overall the soil looks wetter than at the start of the year.
causes: Irrigation and flooding of fields for crops
Seasonal rainfall and rising water tables
properties.why_it_matters: Wetter soil can affect crop health and how salty the land becomes over time.
properties.next_step: Compare with crop calendars and irrigation schedules.
properties.explanation:
Radar is sensitive to water in the soil: wetter ground reflects the signal differently. Across this region the signal grew steadily stronger through the year, with a small seasonal wobble.

That is consistent with a combination of irrigation and a higher water table. Farmers flood fields on a schedule, so some of the movement is simply the farming calendar.

This is a trend worth watching rather than a warning. If moisture keeps rising, soil salinity could become a concern.

properties.headline: Rapid ground change at new city construction east of Cairo
properties.subtitle: New urban development
properties.summary: This patch of desert became much brighter on radar around mid-year. That sudden jump is the signature of buildings and roads appearing.
causes: New buildings and roads replacing open desert
Large earth-moving works
properties.why_it_matters: Fast urban growth changes water demand, traffic and how the ground behaves.
properties.next_step: Confirm with high-resolution optical imagery.
properties.explanation:
Hard, angular surfaces like walls and roofs bounce radar straight back to the satellite, so built-up areas look very bright. Here the signal jumped by about 3.8 decibels over just a few passes.

A sudden step like this is different from slow natural change. It is consistent with construction starting across a large area.

A photo from another satellite could confirm what is being built.

properties.headline: Lake shoreline shifting with water levels
properties.subtitle: Reservoir shoreline
properties.summary: The lake edge has pulled back from where it was in January, which suggests the water level has dropped.
causes: Seasonal release of water downstream
Less inflow during the dry months
properties.why_it_matters: Lake levels affect water supply, power generation and farming downstream.
properties.next_step: Compare with dam operation records.
properties.explanation:
The shoreline of this large reservoir is easy to track because water looks dark on radar. Over the year the edge retreated, which means the water level fell by an estimated 1.8 metres.

Reservoir levels naturally rise and fall with the seasons and with how much water is released. This pattern is consistent with a normal drawdown, though operation records would be needed to be sure.

properties.headline: New farmland expanding west of the lake
properties.subtitle: Desert reclamation
properties.summary: Patches of desert west of the lake are changing in a way that fits new crops being planted and irrigated.
causes: New irrigated fields being planted
Pumped water feeding reclaimed desert land
properties.why_it_matters: Large new farms use a lot of water and change the local landscape.
properties.next_step: Check with optical imagery to confirm the crops.
properties.explanation:
Growing plants and wet soil change how radar bounces back. West of the lake, signals in several round patches shifted in a way consistent with irrigated crops.

Radar only sees plants indirectly, so confidence is lower here. An optical satellite image would show green fields clearly and confirm it.

properties.headline: Mexico City ground keeps sinking
properties.subtitle: Dense urban area
properties.summary: The city sits on an old lake bed. The radar shows the ground dropping steadily, fastest in the south-east.
causes: Groundwater pumped from the clay beneath the city
Soft lake-bed soil compacting
properties.why_it_matters: Uneven sinking can crack pipes, roads and buildings.
properties.next_step: Compare with groundwater pumping records.
properties.explanation:
Between January and October the radar measured ground movement of -30 mm per year across about 220 km².

This pattern is consistent with groundwater pumped from the clay beneath the city, and possibly soft lake-bed soil compacting. This does not prove a cause.

Why it matters: Uneven sinking can crack pipes, roads and buildings.
